ENCLOSURE 1
Flowers, Keowee Toxaway
By DR. C. LELAND RODGERS Chairman, Department of Biology Furman University
By DR. C. LELAND RODGERS
The Keowee-Toxaway property of Duke Power Company is a tract of approximately 120 500 acres. The company started accumulating the land around the turn of the century after most of the individual landholders had moved away. In 1964 Duke acquired an additional 65,000 acre tract from The Singer Company, and since that time has acquired other tracts as well. In particular, the property is rich in two natural resources-water and timber.
High rainfall, of course, is responsible for the abundance of water for generating electricity and supporting the lush vegetation. In some years it exceeds 100 inches per year. The mean annual precipitation from eleven stations along the rim of the escarpment where the major streams arise varies from 72.9 to 85.3 inches
The major streams originate in North Carolina and flow down the south slope of that part of the Blue Ridge Mountains lying astride the South Carolina-North Carolina state line. From east to west the streams are Eastatoe Creek, Toxaway River, Horsepasture River, Thompson River, and Whitewater River. All of them have cut deep gorges through a part of their course, particularly as they decend the escarpment, a descent of nearly 2000 feet.
As a part of the Southern Appalachians the forests contain more species of plants than the deciduous
forests bordering them.
This is taken as evidence that plants survived here during the recent ice age after which they dispersed into surrounding areas. Furthermore, Keowee-Tozaway is a meeting ground for plants adapted to lower elevations and milder climates and those adapted to higher elevations and harsher climates as is the case in the Southern Appalachians.
An unusually large variety of plants grow here, not only because of the geographical advantages just mentioned but also because of an abundance of habitats resulting from contrasting ecological situations such as elevation, slope, and exposure. In all, over 600 kinds of plants have been collected and identified over a period of several years. Financial support for much of the field work was given by National Science Foundation Grant No. C-17006, administered by Highlands Biological Station.
A few noteworthy plants, either because of their limited distribution or rarity, are as follows:
Shortia galacifolia T. & G.—Oconee Bells. Hymenophyllum tunbridgense (L.) Smith — Tunbridge Filmy-fern.
Trichomanes petermi Gray-Dwarf Filmy-fern. Collinsonia verticillata Baldw. ez Ell. — Whorled
Collinsonia. Pachysandra procumbens Michz. - Alleghany Spurge.
Lysimachia fraseri Duby-Loosestrife.
Stuartia ovata (Cav.) Weath.-Mountain Camellia.
Oenothera perennis L.—Sundropa.
The vascular plants in the following list are grouped in families. A common name is given after each scientific name. The list is substantially complete for the mountains and foothills of Oconee. Pickens, Greenville, and Spartanburg Counties as well as for the adjacent North Carolina counties of Jackson, Transylvania, Henderson, and Polk.
